## Overview

The Bank of Japan's (BoJ) projected policy normalisation in 2026 represents a structural break in the global monetary architecture. After nearly a decade of zero or negative interest-rate policy and yield-curve control, a deliberate hiking cycle compresses the interest-rate differential that has historically funded an estimated hundreds of billions of dollars in yen-denominated carry positions. The carry trade — borrowing in yen at near-zero rates and investing in higher-yielding assets denominated in US dollars, emerging-market currencies, or risk assets — is the principal conduit through which BoJ policy transmits to global financial conditions. A sudden repricing of this trade is not merely a bilateral FX event; it propagates through covered-interest-parity (CIP) deviations, cross-border bank funding lines, sovereign debt markets, and equity valuations in a manner that is simultaneous, non-linear, and frequently obscured by latent common factors [9]. This report presents a multi-layer contagion modelling framework that jointly quantifies the impact of the 2026 BoJ hiking cycle on (i) the currency and sovereign-debt markets of Turkey, Egypt, and Pakistan, and (ii) US technology equities, which are the most duration-sensitive and leverage-exposed segment of global equities.

The transmission mechanism is best formalised through the uncovered interest parity (UIP) condition, augmented by a time-varying risk premium that accommodates CIP deviations. For a yen-funded carry position into a target currency $j$, the expected excess return is:

$$\mathbb{E}_t[R_{carry}^{(j)}] = \left(i^{(j)}_t - i^{JPY}_t\right) - \mathbb{E}_t[\Delta s^{(j)}_{t+1}] + \rho^{(j)}_t$$
